abstract: Building on the Pontryagin Minimum Principle (PMP)–Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) correspondence, second-order differential relations are derived to construct loss terms for neural guidance training. While zerothand first-order terms provide standard supervision for the value function and its gradient (costate), the proposed second-order formulation enforces physics consistency without requiring Hessian ground-truth labels, state-transition-matrix propagation, or additional adjoint generation. The framework is evaluated on an Earth-to-Venus low-thrust trajectory optimization problem. Compared with zeroth- and first-order supervision, the second-order formulation improves the accuracy of guidance reconstruction, residual consistency, and closed-loop robustness.

blocks.html: Value-function learning for guidance could use 0th- and 1st-order supervision [1], whereas higher-order structure is rarely exploited because direct Hessian labels, statetransition-matrix propagation, or auxiliary adjoint data are hard and expensive to compute. The differentiated identities used in this paper are direct consequences of the classical PMP-HJB correspondence. The contribution of this work is to organize those identities into trainable residual losses that can be evaluated from the neural value surrogate and the known dynamics alone, making second-order supervision practical without additional second-order gradient truth data.

blocks.html: At every point where V is differentiable, Eq. (6) and Eq. (5) involve the same pointwise Hamiltonian minimization. Comparing the minimizing arguments shows that, along an optimal characteristic, λ(t) = ∇xV (t, x∗(t)). This identification is stated explicitly in the low-thrust guidance setting by Izzo and Öztürk [4], and it is the key relation that allows a learned value function to generate both costates and feedback controls. In this sense, PMP is trajectory-based and boundary-value oriented, whereas HJB is state-space based and feedback oriented. Accordingly, throughout this paper we assume that V is differentiable on the domain of interest. For problems whose unsmoothed optimal control is bang-bang, this regularity assumption can be supported in practice by standard smoothing or homotopic regularization of the control law or running cost; see, for example, Jiang et al. [5], Bertrand and Epenoy [6], and Taheri and Junkins [7].

In the numerical comparisons below, we consider three separate training settings: using only L0, using L0 + L1, and using L0 +L1 +L2. The last setting is the special case of Eq. (19) with w0 = w1 = w2x = w2t = 1.

This section specializes the general framework to a single low-thrust interplanetary transfer. We consider an Earthto-Venus orbit-insertion example following Izzo and Öztürk [4]. The spacecraft departs Earth on 2005-05-07, the target orbit is defined from the Venus ephemeris 1.05 years after departure, the initial mass is 1500 kg, the specific impulse is 3800 s, and the maximum thrust is 0.33 N. In the normalized units adopted here, the nominal transfer duration used in the numerical evaluation is 8.8, corresponding to about 1.4006 years or 511.6 days.

The underlying low-thrust dynamics, indirect free-final-time solution, and feedback reconstruction all follow the standard Earth-to-Venus setup in [4] and are omitted here for brevity. For data generation, we use the same backward generation of optimal examples (BGOE) strategy as [4]: starting from one nominal transfer, we generate Ntraj = 10,000 perturbed trajectories and sample K = 100 time points from each trajectory, yielding about 106 labeled samples for supervised training. The same case is then used to compare the three loss settings L0, L0 + L1, and L0 + L1 + L2 across ReLU [8], softplus [9], hyperbolic tangent [10], and SIREN-style periodic activations [11, 12], with closed-loop deployment based on the same PMP control reconstruction used in the reference solution. Figures 1 and 2 provide the generated-sample overview and the compact case-study comparison used in the next section.

Section 3 establishes the common Earth-to-Venus benchmark and the compact comparison plots; this section evaluates whether the added second-order loss terms translate into practical deployment gains. We compare the best L0 + L1 and L0 + L1 + L2 models from the same training sweep and nominal stopping time. Figure 2 already shows the main trend: first-order supervision improves the fuel-use estimate relative to L0, and the second-order term further improves guidance reconstruction while reducing the differentiated costate residual. This benefit is consistent for the smooth activations, with ReLU as the main exception. Figures 3–5 provide three complementary diagnostics for robustness, switching accuracy, and local residual consistency.

blocks.html: Figure 3 reports 300 closed-loop Monte-Carlo rollouts with ∆t = 0.01 and additive state-noise standard deviation 2 × 10−4 on the non-mass states. The ensemble mean and ±3σ position-error tube are smaller for the L0 + L1 + L2 model, indicating improved robustness to accumulated perturbations. Because both models are initialized from the same nominal state and propagated to the same nominal final time, the difference isolates the effect of second-order supervision on closed-loop sensitivity.

Figure 4 compares the switching function near the nominal zero crossing. The profile reconstructed from the second-order model remains closer to the nominal curve in both crossing location and local slope, which indicates more accurate switching-time prediction for the bang-offbang transfer. Here the reference curve is obtained from the nominal costate, whereas the learned curves are reconstructed from λθ = ∇xJθ through the same PMP control law used in the nominal benchmark.

blocks.caption: Local residual map for the differentiated HJB/PMP consistency term rx.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: Figure 5 shows a local x-y slice of the differentiated HJB/PMP residual rx around the nominal mid-transfer state. The L0 + L1 + L2 model exhibits a broader lowresidual region, indicating that the learned value function satisfies the differentiated relation on a larger off-nominal neighborhood. This local consistency is aligned with the improved robustness and switching behavior observed in Figs. 3 and 4. The plotted slice is constructed by mapping local Cartesian targets back to consistent MEE states, so the panel directly probes the neighborhood in which the learned value gradient remains dynamically coherent.

Under the smoothness assumptions adopted in this paper, the differentiated second-order identities are consequences of the PMP-HJB correspondence; the contribution is to convert them into trainable loss terms for neural guidance. This adds physically interpretable supervision without Hessian labels, state-transition-matrix propagation, or auxiliary adjoint generation. In the Earth-to-Venus low-thrust case, the second-order term improves guidance reconstruction, residual consistency, and closed-loop robustness, including tighter Monte-Carlo dispersion, more accurate local switching structure, and a broader low-residual neighborhood around the nominal transfer, supporting broader use of second-order PMP-HJB supervision.
